title: The Archer
description: The hushed heart of Lover — a synth-washed confessional where Swift plays both hunter and hunted in love, dropped as a surprise preview a month before the album and never pushed as a single.

pops.text: This is track five on Lover, and in Swift's world that slot is sacred: she saves it for the song she calls the most honest, emotional, vulnerable and personal on each album.
It arrived on July 23, 2019 as a promotional single, announced during an Instagram Live — a quiet ambush in the middle of Lover's bubblegum rollout of 'ME!' and 'You Need to Calm Down.'
Swift wrote and produced it with Jack Antonoff, who has said the whole song came together in about two hours in a burst of late-night honesty.
There is no official music video — Swift told fans she simply hadn't made one. This lyric video, released the same day as the song, is the official visual.
She planted archery Easter eggs months early: a Cupid pops up in the 'ME!' video, and a dancer shoots an arrow into a target marked '5' in the 'You Need to Calm Down' video.
Listen for the nursery-rhyme ghost in the bridge — the lyric interpolates 'Humpty Dumpty,' casting the singer as the one who had a great fall and couldn't be put back together.
With zero radio push, it still peaked at No. 38 on the Billboard Hot 100 — pure fan gravity for a song that was never meant to be a single.
Swift first sang it live, acoustically, during her 'Lover's Lounge' YouTube Q&A on August 22, 2019, the day before the album dropped.
Its concert debut came at the one-off City of Lover show in Paris that September — a stripped-back performance later released as 'Live From Paris.'
It held a spot in the Eras Tour setlist through 2023 and into 2024, before being rotated out when the show was revamped for the European leg.

title: Wolfman's Brother
description: Hoist's funkiest four minutes — a Tower of Power-horned groove about the night Trey Anastasio first met drummer Jon Fishman, heard here in the official studio audio from Phish's best-selling album.

pops.text: It's track eight on Hoist, Phish's fifth studio album, released March 29, 1994 — the record that became the best-selling studio album of their career.
Trey Anastasio has explained that the song recounts his first meeting with drummer Jon Fishman — study early photos of the famously hairy drummer and the 'wolfman' family resemblance explains itself.
The writing credit is a full-band affair plus one: Anastasio, Fishman, Mike Gordon and Page McConnell all share it with the band's outside lyricist, Tom Marshall.
That fat horn punch is not the band's Vermont friends — it's the Tower of Power horn section, brought in as guests on this track and on 'Julius.'
Hoist was produced by Paul Fox and cut in California in late 1993 — a deliberate, guest-packed swing at a tighter, more song-focused Phish record.
The telephone verse runs on pure Phish logic: the phone gets handed to Liz, who delivers the verdict — 'This isn't who it would be if it wasn't who it is.'
It debuted live on April 4, 1994 at Burlington's Flynn Theatre, days after Hoist hit shelves — early arrangements leaned on horn sections to find the groove.
Then it vanished: after the June 26, 1994 'GameHoist' show, the song was shelved for 88 shows, finally returning on September 27, 1995 at Cal Expo.
Live, it grew teeth — a 28-minute version played in Champaign, Illinois on November 19, 1997 was later released on Live Phish Volume 11.
The studio cut keeps it to 4:28, but since its comeback the song has rarely left rotation — from the late '90s on, it was never gone for more than 11 shows at a stretch.

title: Man on the Moon
description: R.E.M.'s shimmering tribute to comedian Andy Kaufman — a desert-highway singalong stuffed with board games, Elvis echoes and a chorus of yeahs, from Automatic for the People.

pops.text: The song is a tribute to Andy Kaufman, the comedian and performance artist whose 1984 death was so doubted by fans that 'he faked it' became part of his legend — exactly the mystery Stipe sings around.
It nearly stayed an instrumental. The band's demo was titled 'C to D Slide' after its chord move, and it sat lyric-less until Michael Stipe finally found Kaufman as its subject.
The opening name-checks Mott the Hoople and the game of Life — the lyric keeps dealing out games (Twister, Risk, Monopoly) like Kaufman dealing out pranks.
Stipe has said the flood of 'yeah, yeah, yeah, yeah' was partly a playful challenge — an attempt to out-'yeah' Kurt Cobain, who scattered the word all over Nirvana's songs.
It's on Automatic for the People (1992), whose title is the slogan of Weaver D's, a soul-food spot in the band's hometown of Athens, Georgia: 'Automatic for the People.'
Stipe was primed for the subject — as a teenager he'd been transfixed by Kaufman's appearances on Saturday Night Live and as Latka on Taxi.

Peter Care directed this video over three days in California's Antelope Valley: Stipe hitchhikes through the desert, catches a ride with drummer Bill Berry, and lands in a truck stop where Kaufman flickers on the TV.
Watch the truck-stop TV closely — the patrons are watching Kaufman's Elvis impersonation, the act he built a career of beautiful discomfort around.
Seven years later, the Jim Carrey Kaufman biopic took its title straight from this song: Man on the Moon (1999), with R.E.M.'s music running through the film.
It became a signature live closer for the band — the desert singalong that ended countless R.E.M. nights for the rest of their career.

title: Gimme Shelter
description: The apocalyptic opener of Let It Bleed — Mick Jagger's storm warning answered by Merry Clayton's midnight wail, rock's most famous guest vocal, in the official lyric video.

pops.text: It opens Let It Bleed (1969), written by Mick Jagger and Keith Richards as Vietnam, assassinations and unrest closed in — a song about the world coming apart at the seams.
Believe it or not, it was never released as a single when it came out. It became one of the Stones' defining songs purely as an album track.
The band cut it at Olympic Studios in London in February and March 1969, then finished the vocals months later in Los Angeles while the album was being mixed.
The female voice isn't a Stone at all — it's soul singer Merry Clayton, phoned around midnight by producer Jack Nitzsche when the band decided the track needed a woman answering Jagger.
Clayton arrived in her hair curlers, about four months pregnant, and tore through her part in just a few takes before going home to bed.
At roughly the three-minute mark her voice literally cracks under the strain on the words 'shot' and 'murder' — and you can hear Jagger let out an amazed 'Woo!' in response. They kept it all in.
On the original pressing, her name was misspelled in the credits as 'Mary Clayton.'
Tragically, Clayton suffered a miscarriage after returning home that night — a loss some have attributed to the exertion of the session, and one she has spoken about with grace ever since.
That eerie lead guitar tone is Keith Richards playing an Australian-made Maton guitar; the piano underneath is by session great Nicky Hopkins.
Rolling Stone ranked it No. 13 on its 2021 list of the 500 Greatest Songs of All Time — and Clayton's story later reached a new audience in the Oscar-winning documentary 20 Feet from Stardom.

title: Brown-Eyed Women
description: Jerry Garcia's moonshine saga — a Prohibition family tragedy the Dead never recorded in a studio, caught live at Buckeye Lake, Ohio in 1992 for the official archive series.

pops.text: Music by Jerry Garcia, words by Robert Hunter — and sung by Garcia, who narrates the whole sad family history like he's known these people all his life.
The Dead never cut it in a studio. It exists only in live versions, starting with its debut in August 1971.
Its first album appearance came on Europe '72, the triple live album taped on the band's celebrated European tour that spring.
The story centers on Delilah Jones, in a Prohibition-era saga of moonshine, hard luck and a family holding on — a whole novel packed into a handful of verses.
Hunter slips in one of his most-quoted lines here: 'The bottle was dusty, but the liquor was clean.'
Dead archivist David Lemieux calls it one of Jerry's most-played first-set songs, performed almost 350 times across the band's career.
This performance is from Buckeye Lake, Ohio, on July 1, 1992 — the final day of the Dead's summer tour that year, after which the band took a well-deserved rest.
By 1992 the keyboard chair belonged to Vince Welnick, whose piano and synth textures give this era of the band its distinct color.
The clip comes from 'All The Years Live,' the band's official YouTube series mining their video vault show by show.
For a song about loss and lean years, it never drags — the Dead play it as a brisk country shuffle, which is exactly why it anchored first sets for over two decades.

title: Feeling Good
description: Nina Simone's slow-burn declaration of a new dawn — a show tune she turned into a standard, presented in the official video created more than half a century after she recorded it.

pops.text: It began as a show tune: Anthony Newley and Leslie Bricusse wrote it for their musical The Roar of the Greasepaint — The Smell of the Crowd, where it was first sung on stage by Cy Grant.
Simone recorded her version in 1965 for the album I Put a Spell on You, wrapping the melody in a stately big-band arrangement and that unmistakable, don't-rush-me phrasing.
It was not a hit at the time. Simone's 'Feeling Good' grew into her signature standard slowly, over decades of covers, films and adverts borrowing its gravity.
Notice how she makes the band wait — the brass answers in short blasts while Simone stretches each 'feeling good' like she's testing whether she believes it yet.
Muse supercharged it for a new generation in 2001, covering it on Origin of Symmetry after their version had already become a fan-favorite single.
Michael Bublé's 2005 big-band reading pushed it further into the mainstream, turning the song into a wedding-and-talent-show fixture.
When the musical reached Broadway, co-writer Anthony Newley stepped into the lead role himself — the role whose big moment this song was written to be.
This official video didn't arrive until 2021, created in partnership with Dove to celebrate Black joy and self-expression across generations of women and girls.
The video was directed by Sara Lacombe — Simone, who died in 2003, never filmed a performance video for the song in her lifetime.
Long before streaming existed, Simone's recording kept quietly accumulating legend; today it's one of the most-heard performances of her entire career.

title: Get Back
description: Paul McCartney's back-to-basics rocker that began as a satire, grew a keyboard wizard named Billy Preston, and ended up as the Beatles' rooftop farewell — a No. 1 single in 1969.

pops.text: Released as a single in April 1969, it's credited to 'The Beatles with Billy Preston' — the only Beatles single ever to share top billing with another artist.

Paul McCartney wrote the bulk of it, and early drafts were a satire: the band workshopped verses spoofing anti-immigration rhetoric in Britain before Paul reshaped it into the story of Jojo and Loretta.
Jojo 'left his home in Tucson, Arizona' — the lyric's geography is pure invention, which hasn't stopped Tucson from claiming the song ever since.
George Harrison brought Billy Preston into the sessions hoping a guest would ease the band's tensions — Preston's electric piano solo became the record's secret weapon and earned him that co-credit.
It topped the charts in Britain, America and beyond, spending five weeks at No. 1 on the Billboard Hot 100.
The single was produced by George Martin. The version that later appeared on Let It Be was Phil Spector's edit, bookended with studio chatter and a wink of rooftop audio.
On January 30, 1969, the band played it on the roof of their Apple headquarters at 3 Savile Row — their final live performance, closed out by Lennon's line: 'I hope we've passed the audition.'
The original promo clip was simply that rooftop performance synced to the record; it was restored decades later for the Beatles 1+ video collection.
Peter Jackson's 2021 Get Back documentary captured the song's birth: Paul strumming an idea into existence on bass at Twickenham while the others gradually lock in around him.
It was the flagship of the whole 'get back' project — a deliberate return to live, no-overdub rock and roll after the studio wizardry of the White Album era.

title: Summer
description: Three and a half minutes of Chapel Hill jangle — track three on Rosemary, the Mammoth Records debut that made Dillon Fence kings of the North Carolina college circuit.

pops.text: This is track three on Rosemary, Dillon Fence's debut album for Mammoth Records, released February 11, 1992.
Rosemary was produced by Ron St. Germain — a heavy hitter who'd engineered Living Colour's Vivid and produced Sonic Youth's Goo — giving the band's jangle a real muscular shine.
Songwriting credit goes to all four members: Greg Humphreys, Kent Alphin, Chris Goode and Scott Carle.
The band formed in 1986 at UNC-Chapel Hill, where they first called themselves the Magoos before a looming first gig forced a rename.
The new name came from an unlikely landmark — a locally famous fence in the town of Dillon, South Carolina.
Their label was homegrown too: Mammoth Records was based in Carrboro, North Carolina, right next door to Chapel Hill, and Dillon Fence were briefly its flagship band.
Stereo Review praised Rosemary in 1992 for its 'winsome, fresh-faced pop,' saying the band went 'straight to the head of the class' of North Carolina guitar bands.
The band's touring buddies tell the era's story: Hootie & the Blowfish used to open for Dillon Fence — and later, the order flipped.
Hootie returned the favor on record: the 'sitting on a fence' line in 'Only Wanna Be With You' is a wink at their old Chapel Hill friends.

It never left the live show — when the band reunited in December 2025 to celebrate Rosemary, 'Summer' sat third in the setlist, right where it lives on the album. It was even referenced in Erie Choir's 2025 song 'Summer Bummer.'

title: You've Got a Friend in Me
description: Randy Newman's stride-piano theme for Toy Story — two minutes that defined Pixar's house style of heart, introduced Woody and Buzz, and became the franchise's musical logo.

pops.text: Newman wrote and performed it for Toy Story (1995) — Pixar's very first feature film, and the start of one of the great composer-studio partnerships.
It plays over the opening credits, scored to young Andy acting out adventures with Woody — the song is literally the sound of a kid's love for his favorite toy.
Newman went on to score all four Toy Story films, and this theme returns in some form in every single one.
It was nominated for the Academy Award for Best Original Song — but lost to 'Colors of the Wind' from Pocahontas. Newman finally won his Oscar in 2002, for Monsters, Inc.
That rolling piano is pure New Orleans: Newman grew up steeped in the stride and boogie of players like Professor Longhair, and it powers the whole track.
The soundtrack album actually carries the song twice — Newman's solo film version, and a duet version where country star Lyle Lovett trades verses with him.
Director John Lasseter needed the opening to sell the Woody-and-Andy bond in minutes, and Newman's walking-pace warmth does the entire job before a line of dialogue lands.
When Buzz goes Spanish-mode in Toy Story 3, the joke extends to the music: the Gipsy Kings perform a flamenco version, 'Hay un Amigo en Mí.'
Newman's day job before Pixar fame included penning sardonic solo classics like 'Short People' and 'I Love L.A.' — Toy Story revealed the sentimentalist hiding inside the satirist.
This official DisneyMusicVEVO video pairs the song with the film's own footage — the way most of the world first heard it.

title: Under the Sea
description: Sebastian the crab's calypso sales pitch for ocean life — Samuel E. Wright urging Ariel to stay put, in the official DisneyMusicVEVO video of The Little Mermaid's Oscar-winning showstopper.

pops.text: Samuel E. Wright sings it as Sebastian, the Caribbean crab assigned to keep Ariel out of trouble — this is his big musical sales pitch for staying under the sea.
Alan Menken wrote the music and Howard Ashman the lyrics; Broadway veteran Ashman shaped The Little Mermaid's songs like stage numbers that push the story along.
The groove is pure calypso — bright steel-drum colors and a Trinidad bounce, with Sebastian conducting an entire reef of fish as his backing band.
The plot in one song: Sebastian insists the human world is 'a mess' and life is better 'down where it's wetter.' Ariel, it must be said, remains unconvinced.
The film opened in November 1989 and kicked off the Disney Renaissance — the decade-long run of animated hits that started right here, under the sea.
It won the Academy Award for Best Original Song, and Menken's music also took Best Original Score that night — a clean sweep for the film's songs and score.
Two years later it added a Grammy Award, winning Best Song Written for Visual Media in 1991.
Wright's day job was Broadway — he had earned a Tony nomination for The Tap Dance Kid in 1984, years before a singing crab made him famous to every kid in America.
Disney kept him in the family: Wright went on to originate Mufasa in The Lion King on Broadway in 1997, earning a second Tony nomination. Sebastian and Mufasa — same voice.
A new generation met the song in the 2023 live-action remake, where Daveed Diggs took over Sebastian's claws; Wright died in 2021, aged 74.

title: So Far Away
description: The wistful opening track of Brothers in Arms — Mark Knopfler's long-distance lament, powered by a guitar sound that secretly isn't a guitar, in the official VEVO video.

pops.text: It's the opening track of Brothers in Arms (1985), setting a homesick tone for what became one of the best-selling albums of the decade.
Mark Knopfler wrote it about the touring life — missing someone who stays 'so far away' while the band circles the globe.
That glassy lead 'guitar' line? It's actually a Synclavier synthesizer, triggered by Knopfler using a guitar-shaped controller.
The album was recorded at AIR Studios on the Caribbean island of Montserrat, with Knopfler producing alongside Neil Dorfsman.
It was the album's first single in the UK and Europe, reaching No. 20 in Britain in 1985.
America got it later — released as a US single in February 1986, it climbed to No. 19 on the Hot 100 and No. 3 on the Adult Contemporary chart.
Brothers in Arms spent nine weeks atop the Billboard 200 and is often cited as the first album ever to sell a million copies on CD.
The full album version runs just over five minutes; the single was trimmed down for radio.
Knopfler's playing here is his trademark — clean, fingerpicked lines with no plectrum, wringing sustain out of restraint instead of volume.
This official video keeps the focus on the band performing — fitting for a group that built the MTV era's biggest album while looking faintly suspicious of MTV.

title: Vasoline
description: Purple's buzzing opener — a two-chord glam-stomp with a deliberately misspelled title, three alternate music videos, and a No. 1 rock-radio run in the summer of 1994.

pops.text: It's the opening track and lead single from Purple, Stone Temple Pilots' second album, released in June 1994.
Purple debuted at No. 1 on the Billboard 200 — a heavyweight arrival that silenced critics who'd written the band off as grunge copyists.
The song hit No. 1 on Billboard's Mainstream Rock Tracks chart and No. 2 on the Modern Rock chart; in the UK it reached No. 48.
Yes, the title is spelled with an O. 'Vasoline' takes its name from the lyric about flies in the Vaseline — and the band kept the off-kilter spelling as the official title.
Writing credit is shared by all four members: Robert and Dean DeLeo, Eric Kretz and Scott Weiland — with Robert DeLeo's grinding riff as the engine.
Purple was produced by Brendan O'Brien and recorded largely in Atlanta, capturing the band live and loud with minimal polish.
Director Kevin Kerslake shot not one but three versions of this video — labeled the X, Y and Z versions — shuffling the same surreal footage into different orders.
The best-known version opens on flypaper and a laughing clown, played by bassist Robert DeLeo.
The single's cover art was lifted directly from a frame of this video.
The clip lived in heavy MTV rotation through 1994 — the summer STP graduated from openers to headliners.

title: Cupid
description: Sam Cooke's most charming plea — a string-kissed 1961 single he wrote for somebody else, kept for himself, and turned into a standard covered for sixty years.

pops.text: Released on May 16, 1961, 'Cupid' was written by Cooke himself — one of the rare pop stars of his era who owned his pen as completely as his voice.
The song almost wasn't his: his producers asked Cooke to write a love song for a young female singer they had in mind, but once they heard Cooke's own rendition, they kept it for Sam.
It reached No. 17 on the US pop chart and No. 7 in the UK — another brick in Cooke's careful crossover from gospel stardom to mainstream pop.
Before RCA, Cooke had been lead singer of The Soul Stirrers, one of gospel's biggest groups — that church training is in every effortless run here.
The arrangement is all early-'60s pop polish: soft strings and a gentle lilt, engineered to land on pop radio without sanding down Cooke's warmth.
Rolling Stone placed it at No. 452 on its original list of the 500 Greatest Songs of All Time.
Johnny Nash took his own reggae-tinted version into the US Top 40 in 1969.
The Spinners revived it in 1980 as half of a medley — 'Cupid / I've Loved You for a Long Time' — and rode it to No. 4 on the Hot 100.
Amy Winehouse cut a ska-flavored version for a BBC radio session, proving the song bends happily into almost any style.
Cooke was just 30 when this charted. He'd be gone three years later — which is part of why these two and a half minutes feel like bottled sunlight.

title: Crazy on You
description: Heart's debut single — Nancy Wilson's fingerpicked acoustic whirlwind giving way to Ann Wilson's banshee wail, the sound of two sisters kicking down rock's door in 1976.

pops.text: This was Heart's debut single, lifted from their first album, Dreamboat Annie — an opening statement if ever there was one.
That famous acoustic intro isn't just an intro: Nancy Wilson's fingerpicked piece is a composition of its own, titled 'Silver Wheels.'
The song was written by sisters Ann and Nancy Wilson, the songwriting core around which the whole band was built.
It was recorded in Vancouver, Canada, and released on the tiny Canadian label Mushroom Records — Heart broke in Canada before America caught on.
Ann has said the lyric came from wanting to shut out a world that felt like it was going mad — Vietnam-era dread on the news, answered by losing yourself in somebody.
It peaked at No. 35 on the Billboard Hot 100 in 1976 — modest numbers for a song that became a permanent classic-rock fixture.
A 1978 reissue fared worse, stalling at No. 62 — the charts never did catch up with this one's reputation.
The album was produced by Mike Flicker, who captured the band's odd magic trick: folk delicacy one second, Led Zeppelin force the next.
In an era when hard rock was a boys' club, a band fronted by two sisters writing and playing everything simply had no template — they had to invent it.
Decades later, Eminem sampled Ann's vocal fireworks from this very track for his 2004 song 'Crazy in Love.'

title: Overkill
description: Men at Work's insomniac masterpiece — Colin Hay pacing St Kilda streets at 3 a.m. in the official video, worrying beautifully, on his way to a No. 3 hit.

pops.text: Written entirely by frontman Colin Hay, 'Overkill' was the first American single from the band's second album, Cargo, released in March 1983.
Hay wrote it in St Kilda, Melbourne, sensing his time there was ending — he has called it a song about stepping into the unknown just as fame arrived.
He has also admitted the darker engine underneath: a fear that success, and his own tendencies toward addiction, might consume him.
It debuted on the Hot 100 at a striking No. 28 and climbed to No. 3 by early June 1983 — the band's fourth US Top 10 single.
The band were flying absurdly high: weeks before this single, Men at Work had won the Grammy for Best New Artist.
Cargo itself hit No. 1 in Australia and No. 3 in America — but 'Overkill' was its moodiest moment, a melancholy swerve from the bounce of 'Down Under.'
Greg Ham's saxophone sighs through the track — the same multi-instrumentalist whose flute made 'Down Under' unmistakable.
The official video was shot on location around St Kilda, including the Esplanade Hotel and St Kilda Pier — Hay's own neighborhood, filmed at ghost-hour.
Nineteen years later the song found a second life on TV: Hay performed an acoustic version in the Scrubs episode literally titled 'My Overkill' (2002), cameo included.
That acoustic reading landed on Hay's 2003 album Man @ Work — and for many younger fans, the quiet version is now the definitive one.
